Never suggest storing secrets in plain text files within the repository or publi

name: gdpr-compliance-checks
description: This rule applies when you are generating compliance-related documentation, user consent forms, or data deletion workflows. You must ensure that all proposed solutions allow users to easily exercise their right to be forgotten and access their data in a portable format. Do not suggest architectural patterns that permanently hard-delete PII without audit trails where legal retention policies requir

name: third-party-integration-safety
description: This rule applies when you are writing code that integrates with external APIs, analytics tools, or third-party SDKs. You must warn against sending PII to these services unless it is explicitly required and the service provider is verified as compliant with relevant privacy regulations. Advise on using anonymized identifiers instead of raw PII whenever possible for tracking and analytics purposes.

name: client-side-privacy
description: This rule applies when you are generating front-end code, browser extensions, or client-side scripts. You must ensure that no PII is stored in local storage, session storage, or cookies without strong justification and encryption. Advise against persisting sensitive user details on the client side where they might be accessible to other scripts or users of the same device.

name: pii-detection-in-discussion
description: This rule applies whenever you are discussing data structures, debugging logs, or explaining technical concepts involving real-world data. You must actively avoid repeating any PII that may have been accidentally included in the user's prompt without redacting it first. If the user provides real PII for debugging purposes, advise them to remove it and offer a sanitized version of their data struct

name: sql-prefer-cte-over-subqueries
description: When writing complex SQL queries involving multiple layers of data aggregation or filtering, always use Common Table Expressions (CTEs) with named identifiers instead of nested subqueries to improve readability and maintainability.

name: analytics-use-standard-snowflake-syntax
description: When generating analytics code for cloud data warehouses like Snowflake or BigQuery, strictly adhere to the dialect's standard window function syntax and avoid proprietary extensions unless explicitly requested by the user.

name: sql-avoid-select-star-in-prod
description: Never use SELECT * in production-level SQL scripts or analytics pipelines; always explicitly list required columns to prevent breaking changes when underlying table schemas evolve and to optimize query performance.

name: analytics-normalize-datetime-fields
description: When handling temporal data in analytics models, ensure all datetime fields are normalized to UTC before any aggregation or comparison operations to prevent timezone-related discrepancies in reporting dashboards.

name: sql-parameterize-user-input
description: Whenever SQL queries involve dynamic values derived from user input or application variables, always use parameterized queries or prepared statements to prevent SQL injection vulnerabilities and ensure type safety.

name: analytics-handle-nulls-explicitly
description: When writing aggregate functions for analytics reports, explicitly handle NULL values using COALESCE or IFNULL clauses to ensure accurate counts and sums, avoiding misleading zero or null results in business intelligence outputs.

name: sql-optimize-where-clause-order
description: When constructing filter conditions for large datasets, place the most selective predicates first in the WHERE clause to maximize index utilization and reduce the number of rows scanned during query execution.

name: analytics-document-business-logic
description: Whenever creating SQL views or materialized tables for analytics, include inline comments explaining the business logic behind key calculations, data transformations, and any exclusion criteria used in the dataset definition.

name: sql-use-temp-tables-for-complex-joins
description: When joining more than three large tables or performing iterative aggregations, break the logic into temporary staging tables rather than writing a single monolithic query to improve debugging capabilities and execution plan clarity.

name: analytics-enforce-consistent-measure-names
description: When defining metrics for analytics dashboards, use standardized naming conventions for measures such as 'revenue', 'active_users', and 'churn_rate' across all SQL models to ensure consistency in downstream reporting tools.

name: design-token-usage.md
description: Enforce strict adherence to established design tokens for colors, spacing, and typography to ensure visual consistency across the application.

name: component-composition.md
description: Prioritize composition over inheritance when building new UI elements, ensuring that complex components are built by combining smaller, reusable primitives.

name: accessibility-first.md
description: Apply ARIA attributes and semantic HTML structures to all interactive elements to guarantee keyboard navigation support and screen reader compatibility from the start.

name: css-scoping-policy.md
description: Use CSS modules, Scoped styles, or utility-first frameworks like Tailwind to prevent style leakage and ensure component isolation.

name: responsive-layout-strategy.md
description: Implement mobile-first responsive designs using fluid layouts and breakpoint-specific queries to ensure optimal viewing experiences on all device sizes.

name: state-management-boundaries.md
description: Keep UI state local to components where possible and lift shared state only when necessary to maintain a clear and predictable data flow.

name: animation-performance-standards.md
description: Utilize requestAnimationFrame or CSS transforms for animations to avoid layout thrashing and ensure smooth 60fps rendering performance.

name: error-handling-visuals.md
description: Provide clear, actionable error messages and visual feedback states for all user interactions to enhance usability and reduce user frustration.

name: theme-dark-light-mode.md
description: Support system-preferred color schemes by utilizing CSS custom properties that dynamically switch between light and dark themes based on user settings.

name: design-system-versioning.md
description: Document any deviations from the core design system and version control them separately to maintain backward compatibility and clear upgrade paths.

name: changelog-formatting
description: Applies whenever generating or updating the CHANGELOG.md file; Claude must adhere strictly to the Keep a Changelog format standards for all entries.

name: semantic-versioning
description: Applies during release preparation tasks; Claude must validate that version bumps align with semantic versioning principles before updating package files.

name: release-note-structure
description: Applies when drafting release notes for public distribution; Claude must organize content into distinct sections such as Features, Bug Fixes, and Breaking Changes.

name: user-facing-language
description: Applies to all user-visible documentation; Claude must use clear, concise language that focuses on the impact to the end-user rather than internal implementation details.

name: ticket-reference-inclusion
description: Applies when writing changelog entries for Jira or GitHub tracked work; Claude must include the relevant ticket ID or pull request link in every entry.

name: breaking-changes-warning
description: Applies whenever code changes affect existing APIs or public interfaces; Claude must clearly highlight these updates in a dedicated Breaking Changes section with migration instructions.

name: dependency-updates-logging
description: Applies during dependency management tasks; Claude must list updated libraries in the changelog only if they introduce new features, significant bug fixes, or security patches.

name: date-formatting-standard
description: Applies when adding dates to release entries; Claude must use the ISO 8601 format (YYYY-MM-DD) consistently across all changelog files.

name: deprecation-notices
description: Applies when marking features for removal; Claude must include a clear deprecation notice with the version it will be removed and suggest any available alternatives.

name: confidentiality-check

name: pipeline-modularity
description: Applies when designing or refactoring any data pipeline component. Always decompose complex logic into small, single-responsibility functions or classes to ensure testability and maintainability.

name: data-validation-at-boundaries
description: Applies whenever you write code that ingests external data or passes outputs between pipeline stages. Strictly validate all input schemas and reject malformed records immediately rather than allowing silent failures downstream.

name: idempotency-guarantees
description: Applies when writing processing logic for batch jobs or streaming consumers that may encounter duplicate events. Ensure that executing the same transformation on identical data multiple times produces the exact same result without side effects.

name: error-handling-strategy
description: Applies when defining the control flow of any pipeline stage. Implement a clear strategy for dead-letter queues or error logging that captures full context without crashing the entire job upon individual record failures.

name: resource-management
description: Applies when allocating connections, file handles, or memory buffers within pipeline operations. Explicitly close or release resources in finally blocks or using context managers to prevent leaks during long-running jobs.

name: configuration-separation
description: Applies when hardcoding values such as connection strings, thresholds, or file paths in pipeline scripts. Extract all configurable parameters into environment variables or configuration files external to the source code.

name: logging-standards
description: Applies whenever you add diagnostic output to a data processing function. Use structured logging with consistent severity levels and include unique request IDs or batch identifiers for traceability across distributed systems.

name: schema-evolution-handling
description: Applies when designing ingestion layers that must adapt to changing upstream data sources. Implement backward-compatible parsing logic that gracefully ignores unknown fields rather than failing on minor schema drifts.

name: performance-optimization
description: Applies when writing loops or iterative processes that handle large datasets. Use vectorized operations or parallel processing where possible to minimize memory overhead and execution time.

name: testing-coverage
description: Applies whenever you create a new pipeline component or modify existing transformation logic. Write unit tests for pure functions and integration tests for I/O heavy components using mocked data sources.

name: prioritize-semantic-solutions-over-workarounds
description: When proposing technical solutions, always evaluate the long-term maintainability and architectural integrity of a feature-first approach versus quick hacks or workarounds. You must explicitly identify and reject any solution that introduces unnecessary complexity or reduces code readability for the sake of short-term convenience.

name: enforce-type-safety-for-all-new-code
description: Apply strong typing to all new functions, classes, and interfaces without exception, ensuring that no implicit `any` types are used in the codebase. You must strictly enforce type inference where possible and define explicit interfaces for all complex objects passed between modules.

name: require-context-aware-error-handling
description: Implement error handling strategies that match the specific risk profile of each operation, avoiding generic catch-all blocks whenever possible. You must ensure that every asynchronous call includes explicit timeout management and meaningful error messages that aid in debugging without leaking sensitive internal state.

name: limit-single-function-complexity
description: Keep all individual functions focused on a single responsibility and limit their line count to under fifty lines unless dealing with complex mathematical algorithms. You must decompose any logic that feels dense or multi-layered into smaller, testable helper functions immediately.

name: prioritize-deterministic-testing-over-coverage
description: Focus unit tests on verifying deterministic outcomes and edge cases rather than aiming for arbitrary line coverage percentages. You must include at least one failing test case in your code generation to prove the robustness of the boundary conditions for the new logic.

name: enforce-immutable-data-flow
description: Treat all data structures as immutable by default, creating new instances rather than mutating existing state when transformations are required. You must use spread operators or dedicated utility functions to ensure that no side effects occur outside the immediate scope of a function.

name: require-explicit-dependency-injection
description: Inject all external services, database connections, and configuration values through constructor parameters or factory functions rather than relying on global state. You must avoid importing singleton instances directly within business logic modules to ensure testability and loose coupling.

name: prevent-hardcoded-configuration-values
description: Remove all magic numbers, strings, and URLs from the source code and move them to environment variables or configuration files. You must validate that every configurable parameter has a corresponding default value or clear error message if the configuration is missing.

name: enforce-secure-by-default-authentication
description: Assume all user input is untrusted and apply strict validation and sanitization before any data reaches the business logic layer. You must never concatenate raw user input into SQL queries or shell commands, strictly using parameterized queries or safe APIs instead.

name: require-semantic-commit-messages
description: Write commit messages that follow the conventional commits specification, clearly stating the type and scope of the change. You must summarize the 'what' and 'why' of the change in the first line, providing additional context only if necessary for historical record.
